topic: Mechanics II: Rotational Motion and Gravitation
description: This module transitions from point-mass mechanics to the study of extended rigid bodies, covering rotational dynamics, torque, and moment of inertia. It also explores gravitation, Kepler's planetary laws, and satellite motion, which are highly tested core concepts in NEET and JEE.

sections.title: Center of Mass and System of Particles
sections.description: Understanding how a system of particles or a rigid body behaves as if all its mass were concentrated at a single point.

key_concepts.explanation: The unique, mathematical point where the weighted relative position of the distributed mass of a system sums to zero. For uniform symmetric bodies, it lies at the geometric center.

An idealization of a solid body in which deformation is zero or so small it can be neglected. The distance between any two given points on a rigid body remains constant in time regardless of external forces.

important_facts.fact: The center of mass of a system of particles moves as if all the mass of the system was concentrated at the center of mass and all external forces were applied directly at that point.
In the absence of external forces, the velocity of the center of mass remains constant, and its acceleration is zero.

sections.title: Rotational Dynamics and Moment of Inertia
sections.description: The study of forces that cause rotation and the rotational equivalent of mass.

key_associations.extra_info: The rotational equivalent of linear force. It is the cross product of the position vector and the force vector (τ = r × F).
The rotational equivalent of mass. It depends not only on the mass of the body but also strictly on how that mass is distributed relative to the axis of rotation.
The rotational analog of linear momentum, defined as the product of Moment of Inertia and Angular Velocity (L = Iω).

scientific_principles.principle_or_law: Law of Conservation of Angular Momentum
scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: If the net external torque acting on a system is zero, the total angular momentum of the system remains constant.
scientific_principles.application: Explains why an ice skater spins much faster when they pull their arms inward (decreasing Moment of Inertia, thereby increasing angular velocity).

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: 1. Parallel Axis Theorem: I = I_cm + Md^2. 2. Perpendicular Axis Theorem: I_z = I_x + I_y.
scientific_principles.application: Used extensively to calculate the moment of inertia of complex shapes about various non-standard axes.

sections.title: Gravitation and Planetary Motion
sections.description: The study of the universal force of attraction acting between all matter in the universe.

historical_events.event: Publication of Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion
historical_events.significance: Johannes Kepler described the kinematics of planetary motion around the sun, which later provided the foundation for Newton's theory of gravitation.

scientific_principles.application: States that every particle attracts every other particle with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers.

scientific_principles.formula_or_statement: 1. Law of Orbits (Elliptical), 2. Law of Areas (Constant areal velocity), 3. Law of Periods (T^2 ∝ a^3).
scientific_principles.application: Used to determine the orbital periods, distances, and velocities of planets and satellites. The Law of Areas is a direct consequence of the conservation of angular momentum.

sections.title: Gravity, Potential, and Satellite Motion
sections.description: Analyzing how gravity behaves near planetary surfaces and the mechanics of orbiting bodies.

key_concepts.explanation: The minimum initial velocity required for a projectile to permanently escape the gravitational sphere of influence of a massive body. Formula: v_e = √(2GM/R).
The velocity required to maintain an object in a stable circular orbit around a celestial body. Formula: v_o = √(GM/r).

important_facts.fact: The value of acceleration due to gravity (g) is not constant. It decreases with altitude above the Earth's surface and with depth below it. It is maximum at the poles and minimum at the equator due to Earth's equatorial bulge and rotation.
For Earth, the escape velocity from its surface is approximately 11.2 km/s, and it is independent of the mass or projection angle of the escaping body.
